about: The words of the chain year_1066 (cards: Data/encounters/chain_year_1066_793.json; page: Design/content/chains/year_1066.md). Written 6 Oct 2026: a draft for the user to overwrite. The lines in the Chronicle's voice are our own renderings of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (C, D, E) for 1066 and of William of Poitiers; nothing is quoted from a modern translation. The skald's half-verse in end_norse is our own, in the period's manner. Every card has an art.<card id> entry for the artist, and every ending an art.chain_year_1066.ending.<name>.

entries.text: The long-haired star
Nobody on the landing is working. There is a star with hair in the evening sky, and a skipper in from London who says he can tell you what it is for.

It stands over the roofs after sunset, a star with a tail like a torch in the wind. It was first seen on the eve of the Greater Litany. Men have stopped pointing at it and started counting the nights.
It shone seven nights from the eve of the Greater Litany and then went. It is weeks gone now and nobody talks of anything else. Every man who saw it has since learned what it meant.
The books call it a comet, the long-haired star. They say it comes for the death of a king. They do not say which king, and this year there is a choice.

King Edward died on the eve of Twelfth Day and was buried in his new church the next morning. Earl Harold was hallowed king the same day, before the candles were out. Quick work, even for the English.
The duke of the Normans says the kingdom was promised to him, and that Harold swore to it on relics. He is not arguing the matter. He is building ships. Rope is very dear at Rouen.
And there is the king of the Norwegians, who has fought everyone from here to the Greeks' city and has an old bargain between dead kings to stand on. He has not said anything. He seldom does first.
Keep clear of the Kentish havens for a month. The king's brother Tostig wintered with the count in Flanders, and he is coming home with ships. He is short of crews, and he is not asking.
Buy the skipper his ale and get all three stories straight, with the names
Give at the church door, as everyone else is doing this week
Stars are the clerk's business. See to the mooring and the cargo

Two pennies of ale buy you three claims to one crown, a warning about the Kentish shore, and a price: rope, sailcloth and pitch will sell at Rouen all summer for half as much again. The star is thrown in free.
Six pennies in the bowl. The crew see it and are easier for it. The beggar at the door says God will remember you, and looks up at the star as if to make sure it heard.
You see to the mooring. The star stays where it is without your help. In all the years of the house nothing in the sky has yet paid a toll or carried a cargo.
Some willingly, some unwillingly
The king's brother has come home from Flanders with a fleet and without the king's leave. His men are going from ship to ship along the haven, and they are not asking for the toll.
Sandwich haven and the channel behind Thanet are full of his sails, Flemish hulls among them. He took money and food on Wight and has burned his way east along the coast since. Now he wants shipmen.
The skipper who talked under the star said this would happen, and when. You paid two pennies for the warning and came here anyway.
Earl Tostig pays a man who comes willingly. A man who has to be fetched comes all the same, and pays his own way. You have a sound ship and a full crew. Which kind are you?
We go north to the Humber, sixty ships. The earl has friends in Lindsey. He says so himself.
I have eleven men and a horn. I blew the horn. There is a creek behind the salt pans where a boat your size could lie four days and see nothing.
The king is in London and ought to hear how many they are and which way they went. I cannot leave. You can. Count them as they pass the point.
Go north with the earl for his pay: sixty ships to the Humber
Slip the mooring on the night ebb and be gone before they reach your berth
Give his man silver to find your ship too small to be worth pressing
Lie quiet with the reeve till the earl sails, then take the count of his ships to the king's men in London

Three weeks. The earl's friends in Lindsey meet him with two earls and an army, and he is driven back to his ships. The shipmen leave him by night, and so do you, with sixty of his pennies and every sandbank of the Humber mouth by heart. He goes on to Scotland with twelve small ships.
No lights, a rag round the oar looms, and the ebb does the rest. By first light the haven is a line of masts astern, and none of them is following.

A guard boat is lying across the channel, and not by chance. You go north with the earl after all, unpaid, and thirty pennies lighter for the trouble you gave. You learn the Humber sands. When the other shipmen leave him, you leave too.
He weighs the purse in his hand and then looks at your ship for some time. He decides she is very small. He is right that it is cheaper than the Humber.

Four days up a creek with the mast down. On the fifth he sails north and you count sixty past the point. At London the king's men have heard it already from three riders. They write your count down anyway, since it is the only one that agrees with itself.
Bread for the ships
The king lies off Wight with more ships and men than any king here has gathered, and every one of them eats. His steward is on the hythe buying corn from anybody who has it.
A ship-force and a land-force greater than any king gathered in this land before. That is how the monks will write it. I write it as loaves, and it comes to a great many.
You are the one who counted Tostig's ships and got the same number twice. The king was told. Sit down.
Thirty loads of wheat landed on this hythe within sixty days. I pay four tenths over the market, in the king's pennies, which are good ones.
You are the Emperor's men. You come in your own ships and the law here holds you as good as a Londoner. King Æthelred's men wrote that down. Nobody has yet written that you will not sell us bread.
I am from Rouen. I sell wine, as my father did, at this same wharf. I also know how to count loaves. Do not look at me like that. Everybody on this river is counting something this summer.
You have counted too: keels on the Seine, yard by yard. The steward does not know that yet. The wine man from Rouen may suspect it.
Take the king's order: thirty loads of wheat landed here, at his price and a good one
Sell him what you counted on the Seine: the duke's keels, by yard and by week
A king's order is paid when the king wins. Decline, civilly
He cuts a tally and you take your half. Thirty loads by sixty days, four tenths over. The wine man from Rouen watches the stick change hands and goes on rinsing a measure.

He hears it through twice and has a clerk put it on wax: how many keels, how far planked, and how many weeks until they can swim. A hundred and twenty pennies. He says the king will want to hear it from the man who saw it.
He nods. He has heard it from better men than you this week, and expects worse before harvest. He goes on to the next ship.
Every hull that floats
Both banks below the bridge are shipyards this year. A clerk with wax tablets comes down your gangplank before the mooring is made fast, and looks at the ship before he looks at you.
I serve the duke's steward. The duke takes every hull that floats, and he pays for it. I am told to say both parts, in that order.
Rope first. Then pitch, sailcloth and iron for rivets. Twenty coils of rope landed here inside sixty days, and I pay six tenths over what the market asks. The market has stopped arguing with me.
These ships were trees at Easter, with the leaves on. Green oak, and split, not sawn. They will swim one summer and cross one sea. Nobody has asked me for more than that.
A hired ship lies with the fleet from the first week of September until the wind serves. It does not leave before the wind does. I say this now so that nobody need say it to you later with a spear.
There is half of a tally stick in your chest for the English king's bread. The clerk has not asked what else you carry, and it would be a poor moment to tell him.
Take his order for rope: twenty coils, landed here, at six tenths over the market
Put the ship at the duke's hire for the crossing: silver now, the rest on the far shore
Sell him nothing. Walk the yards, drink with the wrights and count keels
He writes you down between a man from Caen and a man from Bruges. Twenty coils, sixty days, six tenths over. Rope is rope, he says. It does not know whose anchor it holds.
Two hundred pennies, counted out on your own hatch. She is to be with the fleet in the first week of September, with stalls built for six horses. The rest is to be paid, he says, on the other shore.

The wrights drink like men paid by the keel. By dark you know every yard from the bridge to the bend, how many hulls stand in each and how far planked. They can swim by Lammas. Nobody saw you count, or nobody who was sober.
A sergeant finds you pacing out a slipway. He walks you back to your ship, very politely, and charges twenty pennies for the walk. You have half a count, and half a count is a guess.
Half the levy of the land

Ships have been going north up the sound for nine days, to a gathering in the Solund isles. The king's man on the landing wants two things of a foreign skipper: food, and what he knows of the English rivers.
They go by in tens and twenties, shields inboard and sails patched, farm boats rowing after them with the last sack of meal. Nobody on the landing cheers. They are counting who is aboard.

The king has called out half the levy of the whole land. That is one man in two who can pull an oar, and the ship to put him in. The English earl has promised him friends over there. We will see how many.
We know the sea road. Shetland, Orkney, then down the coast. What we lack is a man who knows the river to York: where the sand lies in the Humber, and how far up the Ouse a long ship floats.
You were in the Humber this spring with the English earl. It is a small sea and men talk. Then you have seen the sands, and you can tell me whether he has any friends there.
If he pays you in the king's pennies, bite one. They are one part silver and two parts kettle. A man who served the king nine years threw his pay on the floor in front of him. Ask for it by weight.
My husband and my eldest are both gone north. Every farm on this sound has sent a man. The king has been at war for thirty years and it has not killed him yet. I say that to myself each night.
Sail with them as a pilot for the Humber and the Ouse, for silver by weight
Sell him ship's bread and stockfish, and argue for weighed silver, not counted pennies
Wish him a fair wind, and keep your keel out of it

A hundred and fifty pennies' weight of hack silver and broken rings, weighed on your own scales. You are to lead the fleet in past the Spurn sands when it comes, in September. You will be at York when the ships are.
He argues for an hour and then sends for the scales. Seventy pennies' weight in cut silver. The farm wife, passing with a pail, does not look at either of you.
He pays in the king's pennies, very new and very many. The farm wife was right. Melted down they are worth twenty-five. You have heard the king has a hard hand. It seems he also has a thin one.
He shrugs and goes back to his tally. With the men gone, the farms will sell their cloth cheap for bread until spring. The farm wife says so herself, and what she will take for it.
The food is gone
The steward has no corn to buy and no silver left to buy it with. The ships have lain off Wight since May. On Our Lady's birthday the men will be let go home, unless somebody feeds them on trust.
The men's food is eaten and no man can keep them there longer. They have reaped nothing at home all summer. The duke has not come. They say he never will, and that their barley is rotting.
Three weeks' bread would hold them past Michaelmas. After Michaelmas nobody crosses that water with horses. I cannot pay you until the king's rents come in. I can only tell you that he pays.
You filled the first order to the day, which is more than my own reeves did. So I ask you before I ask the others.
There is corn on the Rhine. The harvest was good and the barns at Tiel are full. Six hundred pennies down would load our keels, if a house we know goes first. We follow a house we know.
A king's debt is a good debt while there is a king. I have seen four kings of the English in this town. Think about the wind as well. Corn that comes a week late is only corn.
You know what the steward only fears: how many keels the duke has, and that they could swim by Lammas. He has not sailed because the wind has not let him. That is the only reason.
Stake 600 d, and tell him to the keel what the duke has and when it can sail: let the king open the minster barns on that
Stake 600 d of the house's silver on Rhine corn, and every keel of the Emperor's men that will follow you
Put in 150 d with the others, for the ships that are coming home, and promise nothing
No. Men who cannot be fed go home, and that is not a merchant's to mend

You put the silver down and then the count beside it. The steward rides that night. Within the week the bishops' barns in Kent are opened by the king's writ, and eleven keels of the Emperor's men come up the Thames with Rhine wheat. The ships stay off Wight. Whoever writes this year down will have to write it differently.

Nine days. Eleven keels come over from the Rhine mouth with a fair wind, and the corn goes down the river to Wight in the king's own boats. On Our Lady's birthday the men are fed, and they stay. The elder says he has never seen the like, and that he would not do it twice.

The wind sits in the west for eleven days. When the corn comes the ships are already coming up the river, those that are coming, for some were lost on the way. The steward buys it for the city at what the city will pay. You have 380 of your 600 back, and his thanks.

It feeds the crews as they come up the river. On Our Lady's birthday the men were let go home, and the king rode up from the coast. You are paid at Michaelmas with forty pennies over. By then it does not matter to anybody.
On Our Lady's birthday the men were let go home, and the ships were sent up to London. Many were lost before they came there. The steward does not hold it against you. He has no time to.
Waiting for a south wind
The duke's fleet lies in the mouth of the Somme under the abbey of Saint Valery, and the wind has blown from the north for two weeks. A sergeant sends you round to join it, loaded or empty.

The Canche is full of the duke's stragglers. The fleet itself lies a tide to the south, in the Somme. You are sent round, and by evening you are anchored among more ships than you have seen in your life.

The Seine yards are empty and the wrights are drunk. The fleet went up the coast to the Somme a fortnight ago. You are sent after it, and two days later you anchor among more ships than you have seen in your life.
You are on the list: hired at Rouen, two hundred paid. Six horses, and their grooms, who will be sick. Do not let the grooms near the steering oar.

A ship that lies in the duke's water, waiting on the duke's wind, is the duke's ship. He pays for it. Two hundred and fifty to carry six horses over. I would take it. The other way of asking is worse.

We lost ships coming up from the Dives, and the men in them. They buried them at night so the army would not count. The guard boats row the bar from dusk to dawn now. That is for us, not for the English.

The duke has asked for our saint to be carried out of the church and set down on a cloth in the open, where the whole army can kneel. He watches the weathercock on our roof more than he watches the altar. He pays for what his men eat, I will say that.
Nobody here knows that the English ships were not sent home. You know it. You paid for the bread.
Take the horses aboard and cross with the fleet when the wind comes round
Slip out on the night ebb with the count of his ships, and run for the English shore
Sell the camp what it will eat, at the duke's fair price, and be gone before the wind changes

Two days before Michaelmas the weathercock turns. You sail at dusk behind a lantern on the duke's masthead, with six horses stamping on the bottom boards. At the third hour of the day the keel takes the shingle at Pevensey. No English ship is there, and no English spear.

You go out with the ebb, between two guard boats that are shouting at each other. At Dover the reeve pays eighty pennies for the count and sends a rider north with it. The king, he says, is at York, fighting somebody else.

A guard boat lays a grapnel on your quarter before you reach the bar. Sixty pennies for the duke's trouble, and six of his horses in your hold for nothing. You cross with the fleet after all, behind the lantern, with a sergeant sitting on your sea chest.
Sixty pennies, paid at once, by a clerk who writes down everything the army eats. On your way out you count the masts. You lose the count somewhere past six hundred.
The Sunday before the bridge

York has given hostages to the king of the Norwegians and has not been burned. His ships lie ten miles down the Ouse. On the staith a carter is telling anyone who will listen what he saw on the Tadcaster road.

On Saint Matthew's eve the two earls met the Norwegians outside the city, at the ford, and were beaten. Men say you could cross the ditch there on the dead. York has agreed to feed the victor and to march south with him.
You brought them in yourself, past the Spurn sands and up the Ouse as far as a long ship floats. They have been pleased with you ever since. It is not altogether a comfortable thing.

I came by the lanes. The road is shut. King Harold is at Tadcaster with an army I could not see the end of. They stop every man going north, so that nobody runs ahead of them. Nobody here believes me. Do you?
Tomorrow we go to the bridge on the Derwent, to be given the hostages of the whole shire. Two men in three go, and one stays with the ships. It is hot. Nobody wears mail to count hostages.
The English king is in the south, watching the sea for the Bastard. Everybody knows that. He cannot be in two places. Kings cannot. I have served one for twenty years, and he has tried.
You are a foreigner, and you have been among them. I will not say whose man I am. Where do their ships lie, how many stay with them, and where do the rest go tomorrow?
Go down the river to the ships tonight and tell the king's men what the carter saw
Tell the thegn where the ships lie, and that the Northmen go to the bridge tomorrow without their mail
Say nothing to anyone. Shift the berth upriver and keep the hatch shut

They laugh until you name the carter's village and the colour of the banners he saw. Then an old man with a scarred mouth goes to wake the king. By dawn the whole host is going to the bridge, and it is going in its mail. Whatever is written of tomorrow, it will not be that they were taken unawares.

They give you ale and laugh. A Frisian frightened by a carter, they say. On Monday they went to the bridge in their shirts, and King Harold came on them unawares. You told them. You are one of very few men alive who know it.

He listens without moving and gives you sixty pennies from his own purse. On Monday King Harold went through York without stopping and came on them beyond the bridge, unawares. It would have gone so without you, most likely. You will never know.

You lie two bends up the river with the hatch shut. On Monday the army goes through the city, and by evening the news comes back. You sold nothing and you told nobody anything. Both kings would call that wise.
After the battle
The king is dead on a hill above Hastings, and two of his brothers with him. The duke's army has come along the coast taking the harbours one by one, and half of it is now too sick to stand.

Dover gave itself up before it was asked, and was burned anyway, by squires after plunder. The duke has paid for the houses. He has not paid for anything else. The smell from his camp is of sickness, not of fire.
Dover gave itself up and was burned anyway. Sandwich has sent its keys. Here on the Wantsum the ferrymen take pennies from both sides and keep their boats on the Thanet bank at night.

It is the water here, and too much fresh meat. Half the army cannot ride. The duke leaves his sick behind and goes on. I need them carried home, and I need flour, since our bread at least does not kill us.
You carried horses over. I have it written. The duke remembers who carried horses. He is busy just now, and has not yet remembered what he owes for them. Come to London at midwinter.
My husband went with the king and has not come back. They are giving the land to men with other names. I have a boy and a girl, and a cousin at Ghent. I have this brooch. I do not have a fare.
You carried word to the king's men this year, and it was written down. It lies in a chest in London now, with everything else King Harold knew.
Carry the duke's sick over to Normandy, and take his order for flour on the way back
Take the widow and her children over to Flanders, and ask no fare
Buy what the fire and the foragers left: eight bolts of wool cloth for 60 d
Fill the water casks and go. There is no market here this month

A hundred and twenty pennies for a hold full of grey-faced men, who are quiet the whole way over. The order is for twenty loads of flour inside forty days, at six tenths over. The sergeant says again that you should come to London at midwinter.

She sits on the thwart with a child under each arm and does not look back at the land. At Ghent her cousin is on the quay. She has left the brooch on the thwart. The boy asks your steersman what every rope is called.
Eight bolts for sixty pennies, with the smoke still in them. The man who sells them is not the man who wove them. Several people watch you carry them aboard. One of them is the widow.
You water from a spring above the town, well away from the camp, and leave on the ebb. There are places a merchant does no good by staying. This is one of them, this month.
Twenty-four ships
The king of the Norwegians is dead at the bridge, and Earl Tostig with him. What is left of three hundred crews is at the ships, sworn to peace and waiting to be told how many hulls it may take home.

King Harold came on them unawares beyond the bridge, and the fight lasted far into the day. The king's son Olaf and the earl of Orkney have sworn to keep peace with this land for ever. Then King Harold went south in haste.
You brought them up this river. You know which ships these were when they were full. Some of the men at the oars now are boys who were left to mind the kettles.
We came with three hundred ships. The English king has counted us and says twenty-four will carry what is left. He counts well. I have gone over it twice myself and cannot make it more.
There are more hurt men than there are benches to lay them on. I am from the Karmsund. So are nine others who cannot row. We have nothing to pay you with. They took even the rings.
The king had the news at table: the duke has landed in the south, at Pevensey, on Michaelmas eve. He was on the road the same day. I am left here to count ships and see them gone.

There is mail for sale behind the tanners' sheds, and swords, cheap. I have not seen it. Mind that the toll man at your next harbour has not seen it either. They look hard at mail in a merchant's hold.
Take as many of the hurt as the ship will hold home to the Karmsund, for nothing
Buy the dead men's mail and swords from the men who stripped them: 120 d the lot
Leave it. Run south with the news while it is still worth a cup of wine

Ten men on the bottom boards, and a late crossing of the North Sea with the wind rising. One dies off the Naze and is put over the side with a prayer in two tongues. The rest will see the sound. They say very little. One of them asks the name of your house, and says it over twice.
Two mail shirts and four swords for a hundred and twenty pennies, a fifth of what they are worth. One shirt has a hole in it the width of a spear. Somebody on the Karmsund paid a farm for that shirt.

A Humber skipper pays thirty pennies to hear all of it first, with the names. News is the one cargo that takes up no room and spoils fastest. By the time you reach the Thames, the other news will have met it coming north.
The ships that stayed
The king's ships were still at sea at Michaelmas, on your corn. The duke's fleet came over in the dark on a south wind and found them in the way.

This year, two days before Michaelmas, the duke of the Normans put to sea by night with a great fleet. The king's ships met it before the land. Many were sunk, and many were driven ashore. The duke got back to the Somme with what he had left, and the winter shut the sea behind him.
He had a lantern at his masthead, so that his own ships could follow him in the dark. So could we. I never saw a kinder thing done at sea.
Some of them came ashore at Romney with their horses, thinking the rest were behind them. The men of Romney did not wait to ask. I ate your bread all through September, master. It was good bread.

The king himself was not there. He was at York, where he killed the king of the Norwegians at a bridge. He came south in eight days ready to fight a second battle, and found that there was nobody to fight.

The king himself was not there. He was thrown back from a bridge near York by Norwegians who were waiting for him in their mail. He holds the south and the sea. He does not hold York. You had some part in that as well.
Six hundred pennies, on trust, in the one week when nobody would lend the king a loaf. He has not forgotten it. He told me to pay it back three times over, and then to ask what else you want.

There is an old rule an archbishop wrote down in King Æthelred's day. If a merchant throve so that he crossed the wide sea three times at his own cost, he was from then on worthy of a thegn's right. You have crossed it rather more often than that.
Ask what the old law gives a merchant who has crossed the wide sea three times at his own cost: a thegn's right
Ask for ground instead: a hythe of the house's own on the Thames
You brought the count of the duke's keels as well as the corn. Ask for the thegn's right and the king's writ on the toll together

Eighteen hundred pennies, and your name is read out as a thegn's before the king's reeves. A thegn's oath counts for six common men's. A thegn also owes the king a ship and its crew when the fleet is called out. The steward mentions this last, and smiles.

Two thousand pennies, and forty feet of the Thames bank below the bridge, with the right to land there and sell from your own ship. You are no man's lord and no man's thegn. You are a house with a hythe in London. Your first forefather had a boat for four men and a debt.

Twenty-six hundred pennies. A thegn's right, with a thegn's ship to find when the king calls. And a writ with the king's seal hanging from it: this house goes free of toll at London, it and its heirs. The steward says the king laughed, and then had it sealed.
Midwinter at Westminster
On midwinter's day the archbishop of York hallows the duke king in King Edward's new church. From the river you hear a great shout inside it, twice, in two tongues. Then there is smoke.

They asked the English in English and the French in French whether they would have him for king, and both shouted yes. The guard outside took the shouting for treachery and set fire to the houses by the church. He was crowned while they burned. He swore to rule as well as the best kings before him.

He is king as far as the Humber. Beyond it a king of the Norwegians is keeping Yule at York. There are two crowns in this land tonight, and a foreign skipper had a hand in that. Nobody in this church knows his name.
I have you on the list of ships. The king pays what the duke owed. He has also laid a tax on the whole land, to pay it with. You need not mention that on the hythe.

Or the king can give what costs him less than silver. A word over his seal. Or ground, of which there is suddenly a good deal with no man on it. Or a hull: we have more transports than we shall ever load again.

The Emperor's men give two grey cloths and a brown one, ten pounds of pepper, five pairs of gloves and two casks of vinegar, at Christmas and again at Easter. King Æthelred's men wrote it down. A new king, and the same toll.
I know what you carried over, and for whom. So does every man on this hythe. We will go on trading with you. A man has to eat. Do not ask us to drink with you as well.
The cloth you bought in the burned town sold well in the end. Wool does not hold smoke for ever. People hold it rather longer.
Ask for the king's word that your house keeps the law it had in King Edward's day, and goes free of the toll
Ask for a hythe whose owner did not come home from Hastings
Ask for nothing a clerk can write. Take the freight you are owed, and one of the transports he no longer needs

Twelve hundred pennies, and a strip of parchment no longer than your hand: this house is worthy of all the law it was worthy of in King Edward's day, and goes free of toll at London, and every child of it shall be his father's heir. It is in English. The king cannot read it either.

Nine hundred pennies, and forty feet of the Thames bank with another man's mooring posts still in it. His widow lives across the lane. She does not curse you. She looks at the posts each morning, as she always has.

Seven hundred pennies, and a transport of green oak with horse stalls still in her. Pull out the stalls and she will carry twice what your old ship did, for as long as her planks hold. You owe the new king nothing. On the hythe that is noticed.
Yule at York

The king of the Norwegians keeps the feast in York, with Earl Tostig on his left hand. His men went to the bridge in their mail, all of them, because a foreign skipper came down the river on a Sunday night.

This year King Harold came upon the Norwegians beyond the bridge and found them ready. The fight lasted the whole day and neither side held the field. In the night King Harold went back to Tadcaster, for word had come to him that the duke had landed in the south.

He fought the duke nineteen days later, with the men he had left, and was killed. So the duke is hallowed king at Westminster this midwinter, and Harald Sigurd's son sits in York. Neither has yet sent the other a greeting.
I have half a verse for it. 'The ring-giver slept light by the river; a Frisian's tongue was his watch-horn.' The second half wants an English king in it. I have not decided which one.
The king pays you by weight, in rings and cut silver. Not in his pennies. He said that himself, and laughed. It is the only time I have heard him joke about the pennies.
He offers a seat among his guests and his peace on your ships in every harbour he holds. Or ground here on the staith. He does not offer both. He says a man with both would be an earl.

We have had Northmen for kings here before. My grandfather's grandfather buried one. They go to Mass in the end, and their sons speak like us. Mind the king in the south, though. He will hear whose guest you are.
Take a seat among the king's guests, and his peace on your ships in every harbour he holds
Ask for ground on the staith by the Ouse bridge, and no seat at anybody's table
You brought his ships up the river as well as the word. Ask for the seat, the ground and the ring from his arm

Fifteen hundred pennies' weight of silver on your own scales, and a seat on the lower bench at the Yule ale. From the Humber to the Lofoten no king's man of his will lay a hand on your cargo. South of the Humber the other king's men have been told your name.

Thirteen hundred pennies' weight, and thirty feet of the staith below the Ouse bridge, paced out by the king's man in the frost. Frisians had houses in this city three hundred years ago, and left them in one night. It has taken the house a while to come back.

The king looks at you for some time. Then he pulls a gold ring off his own arm and says a pilot who can also hear is worth an earl who can do neither. Twenty-four hundred by weight, the seat, the ground, and the Humber is yours to pilot for good. Earl Tostig does not laugh.
The year written down
Midwinter. Three fleets put to sea this year and two kings are dead. The ship is laid up, the men are paid, and what is left is the reckoning.

On midwinter's day the duke is hallowed king at Westminster. From your mooring you hear a shout across the fields, and then you see smoke: his guard has set fire to the houses by the church. On the hythe the toll is what it was at Michaelmas.

Twenty-four ships came home up the sound, of three hundred that went. On the landing they read out no list. The women counted the ships, then the men in them, and then went home, some one way and some another.

The news comes in by the last ships of the year, in pieces and out of order. A king dead at a bridge. A king dead on a hill. A duke hallowed king at Westminster on midwinter's day. The priest writes it on one line.
I have a loom, six ells of cloth and a share in a boat that nobody is left to row. I do not want pennies. I want meal, and a fair measure. They say you give one.

Nine men are alive on the Karmsund who would not be, if your ship had gone south with the news. It was not good trade. Their king's son knows the name of your house, since one of them said it to him twice.
The Kentish widow is with her cousin at Ghent. Her boy has sent word by a wool skipper. He knows the name of every rope now. He asks whether the house has room for one more.
The mail shirt with the hole in it is still in the hold. Nobody has offered for it. The crew step round it.

You fed no king and carried no king's horses, and you still have a ship. Most years that would be nothing to boast of. This year it is. We keep a seat for a house like that. We also drink a good deal. I say so in fairness.
The monks will give this year a page, and it will be all kings. If you want it written the way your house saw it, with what corn cost and who paid, you will have to pay a priest. I am a priest.

It began with a boat for four men and a debt of two pounds to a count, thirteen days after the heathen men came to Lindisfarne. No king has outlasted the house since. Several have tried to borrow from it.
Have the priest write the year down for the house, plainly, with the prices
Take the seat the elder offers among the sworn merchants, and drink the year out with them
Send word to Olaf, Harald's son: the house that carried his father's men home asks his peace for its ships
The Kentish widow's boy has asked to learn the sea. Take him into the house

Seven hundred pennies clear at the reckoning. The priest writes on one skin: 'This year a star with hair was seen, and three fleets put to sea, and wheat stood at such a price at London.' He leaves the kings to the monks. It is rolled up and put in the chest with the scales, for whoever comes next.

Eight hundred pennies clear, and a seat on the bench. They judge their own quarrels, lend to each other without witnesses, and drink at fixed feasts as if it were a duty. A monk once wrote that they were hard men who feared nothing. They have had it read to them, and are pleased with it.

Nine hundred pennies clear. In spring a man comes down the sound with the young king's word: the house's ships go in his peace wherever he is king, and the sound's own pilots will take them through for nothing. They will call him Olaf the Quiet. He builds a market town, and he never once sends a fleet to England.

Seven hundred pennies clear, and a boy of eleven with a Kentish father's name who is sick for two days and then never again. He has kin at Ghent and kin under the new king's hand in Kent. In ten years the house will be glad of both.

This year King Edward died on the eve of Twelfth Day, and Earl Harold was hallowed king. The duke of the Normans is building ships, and the king of the Norwegians is saying nothing. A star with hair was seen for seven nights.
This year the king's ships were not sent home on Our Lady's birthday, for corn came to them from over the sea. They lie off Wight still.
The duke's fleet lies in the Somme under Saint Valery, more than six hundred sail, waiting on a south wind. The duke pays for what it eats.

This year Harald, king of the Norwegians, and Earl Tostig were killed beyond the bridge on the Derwent, and of three hundred ships twenty-four went home. The duke of the Normans landed at Pevensey on Michaelmas eve.
This year the duke of the Normans put to sea by night, and the king's ships met him. He went back to the Somme with what he had left. Harold is king of the English.
This year King Harold was killed near Hastings, and on midwinter's day William, duke of the Normans, was hallowed king at Westminster by Archbishop Ealdred.
This year Harald, king of the Norwegians, kept Yule at York, and William was hallowed king at Westminster. There are two kings in England.
A landing at dusk in a clear April: every head turned up to a comet with a long tail over thatched roofs; a clerk pointing, a weathered skipper with an ale cup, one deckhand still coiling rope.
A Kentish haven on a bright windy morning, crowded with striped sails: an armed housecarl with one foot on a merchant ship's gunwale, an old reeve with a horn standing useless on the shingle behind.
A London hythe at noon in summer: a tired steward splitting a tally stick over sacks of corn; behind him a Rouen wine merchant rinsing a measure and watching; the timber bridge beyond.
The Seine at Rouen on a hot afternoon: both banks lined with half-planked hulls and men with axes, felled oaks in the mud; a clerk with wax tablets stepping onto the merchant's gangplank.
The Karmsund under a grey summer sky: a line of long ships going north with shields inboard; on the landing a king's man with a tally, and a farm wife with a pail watching one ship.
A London storehouse at evening in late summer, the corn bins empty and swept: the steward with open hands, an old merchant in a grey Frisian cloak counting on his fingers, one candle.
The Somme mouth in rain and a north wind: hundreds of masts at anchor; on the shore monks carrying a reliquary out to a cloth on the grass, an army kneeling, a weathercock on the abbey roof.
The staith at York on a hot Sunday evening: a dusty carter talking with both hands, a Norwegian steersman laughing over an ale bowl, a hooded man listening from a doorway; the minster behind.

Dover in a wet October, burned roofs under the cliff and the old Roman lighthouse above: a widow with two children and a small bundle on the shingle, a Norman sergeant with a list, sick men lying under cloaks.
The Ouse below York on a cold clear morning: a long row of empty long ships on the bank, a few being loaded with wounded men; a survivor on a crutch, an English reeve counting hulls on his fingers.
The Channel at first light after a night fight: English ships under oars among wreckage and swimming horses; one distant ship with a lantern still lit at its masthead, heading away south.

Westminster from the Thames on a midwinter afternoon: the new stone church against a red sky, houses burning beside it, mounted guards in the smoke; a merchant ship moored in the foreground, her crew watching.

A hall in York at Yule by firelight: a very tall grey king on the high seat with an English earl at his left, a skald standing; a foreign skipper on the lower bench with scales and cut silver before him.
A merchant's room at midwinter by one lamp: a ship's sail folded on the rafters, a chest open with a pair of scales in it, a priest writing on a single skin while the master of the house dictates.
A London reeve reading out a merchant's name as a thegn's before the king's men; the merchant in a plain cloak among sacks of corn; ships at anchor on the Thames behind.
A hand holding a strip of parchment the length of a palm, a wax seal hanging from it; behind it, out of focus, mooring posts on the Thames bank and a woman looking at them.
A heavy gold arm ring lying in the pan of a small pair of merchant's scales, the other pan empty; firelight, and the shadow of a very tall man across the table.
The landing on the Karmsund in winter dusk: twenty-four long ships drawn up where three hundred sailed, women standing in a line on the shore; one small merchant ship unloading sacks of meal.
